fields.title: Continuity and Change - Mission Quiz
fields.description: Five questions covering the same topics on every attempt. Pass with at least three correct.

fields.title: Change and Continuity Can Happen Together
fields.content:
Change means something becomes different. Continuity means something carries on. A community can experience both at the same time. New institutions, materials or activities do not prove that every earlier skill disappeared. Continuing a skill also does not mean that every use or condition stayed exactly the same.

UNESCO describes Vigan through earlier trading activity and later planning, with architecture drawing on several traditions. This named example helps us ask about layers of history rather than choose between everything changed and nothing changed. Our fictional comparison cards show a familiar skill used for a new purpose. They illustrate a question, not a documented individual workshop. Identify exactly what continued and what changed, then ask what evidence supports each part. One feature cannot explain every community in the islands.

Open the three clues and choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help or revisit the lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs review.

fields.title: Compare the Same Question Across Time
fields.content:
A useful comparison asks the same clear question of sources from different times. A towns beginning, a houses construction and a modern repair are different stages. A later photograph does not automatically show the first form of a building. Nor does a policy date tell us exactly when every community experienced its effects.

Try a fictional source desk with an earlier room plan, a later dated photograph and a repair note. Ask which opening each shows and what changed between them. Before combining them, check that the records concern the same building and feature. Do not compare unrelated houses as if they were stages of one house. A missing feature in a partial image may be outside the frame rather than absent from the building. State what the records show, then identify what still needs evidence. The desk is a model, not an original building archive.

Open the three clues and choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help or revisit the lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs review.

fields.title: A New Rule Was Not Every Outcome
fields.content:
Institutional changes and everyday experiences are connected but different. The 1863 education decree is a named policy development from an earlier lesson. It did not by itself establish identical access, attendance or learning for every child. To explain what changed in a particular town, compare the rule with evidence of what actually happened.

Our fictional cards show a school instruction, a teacher record and a class register. They answer questions about plans, staffing and recorded attendance. None alone proves what every learner understood. Earlier community learning also should not be erased simply because formal schooling expanded. Ask what evidence supports continuity in skills and what supports change in institutions. This comparison does not judge a learners worth or ask students to disclose family resources, religion or school difficulties.

Open the three clues and choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help or revisit the lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs review.

fields.title: People Took Part in Change
fields.content:
People were not simply objects moved by rules. They could make requests, adapt activities, cooperate, contest demands or take other actions within unequal conditions. Having some ability to act did not mean having unlimited freedom or equal power. Explain the action that is recorded without inventing every private motive.

The Bacolor case from an earlier lesson identifies a 1698 petition concerning tribute-collection duties. It shows a particular action within social and institutional relationships. The existence of a petition is not proof that every request was granted or that every community responded the same way. In our fictional comparison, two source cards record different requests in different places. Keep each case attached to its own people, period and outcome evidence. Do not turn a social category into one guaranteed behavior, wealth level or measure of worth.

fields.title: Heritage Can Continue and Change
fields.content:
A living tradition can carry knowledge forward while materials, uses or forms change. A modern heritage object can help us ask about that process. Its modern date should not be hidden to make it appear colonial. An object that looks old is not automatically evidence of every earlier practice.

The Field Museum entry used in the earlier arts lesson dates its named Abel Iloko textile to the early to mid-1960s. That object has a later story of use and memory. It is not a surviving colonial-era textile simply because weaving has a longer history. Our date-and-claim card distinguishes the particular object from a claim about earlier knowledge. To explain an earlier detail, find evidence for that period and attribute community accounts carefully. We do not copy a textile pattern, require a religious practice or treat one owners memory as every families history.

Open the three clues and choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help or revisit the lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs review.

fields.title: Prepare Your Continuity and Change Report
fields.content:
Bring the chapter together. Settlement layouts and houses changed while skills and activities could continue. Teaching materials and policies did not guarantee identical learning. Social categories and local roles did not determine a whole life or human worth. Cultural works have makers, dates and uses. People acted within conditions that could be unequal.

Prepare a fictional report for another Grade 5 learner. State what changed and what continued, identify the people, place and period, give supporting evidence and explain a limit. Compare the same question across sources. Keep a rule separate from implementation, a request separate from success and a modern object separate from evidence of an earlier design. Label the source cards as teaching models and do not invent private conversations.

The main quiz has five questions and three correct passes. Return to linked learning content before practice and a retry if needed. This is the fifth mission, but completing it does not yet complete Chapter 10 or award its final badge. The chapter evidence challenge is still being prepared.
